title: DoorDash's CEO says AI coding is not enough to make engineers more productive
contentSnippet:
Xu said that coding is only a small part of an engineer's day.
Bloomberg/Getty Images

Tony Xu says AI only partly helps DoorDash engineers.
Xu said he wants to see AI integration across all departments, not just engineering.
AI has boosted DoorDash's productivity, with two-thirds of code now generated by models.

Vibe coding is just one small part of the engineering puzzle, says DoorDash's CEO.
"Only certain parts of a software engineer's day are writing code, and it's great that we have models today to write the code for us," Tony Xu said on an episode of the "Uncapped" podcast released Tuesday. "That helps maybe the whatever 25%, 30%, 50% of our time that's actually shipping code."
Xu cofounded the food and grocery delivery giant in 2013. DoorDash went public in 2020, one of the year's biggest tech IPOs.
The CEO said engineers spend another big chunk of time in product reviews, design meetings, and aligning with different business teams. Those aspects require AI too.
"If that doesn't change and come together, you're not going to be able to just have perhaps the productivity gain that you hope to have," he said. "A bunch of companies across the industry are trying to figure out and get those workflows right so that you're not just AI native from code development, but you're AI native in how you actually operate."
For example, the company still needs to work on parts of its business that can be improved with physical AI, such as food-preparation robots and autonomous delivery vehicles, Xu said.
Xu has taken a moderate approach to talking about how AI has changed his company.
During a May earnings call, he said that AI has not yet changed DoorDash's organizational structure.
"We're seeing a lot of productivity gains right now from AI, about well north of half of our code, probably closer to two-thirds of our code is written by AI today," Xu said. "But that doesn't alone articulate how workflows and team setup ought to change."
He joins a handful of tech leaders who have spoken publicly about the limitations of AI and its usefulness to a company.
Earlier this month, Avishai Abrahami, the CEO of Wix, a web design company that acquired the vibe-coding platform Base44, said the tech industry is overselling AI.
"I would love to say the team in three years, we will be a thousand people in Base44 and a thousand people in Wix, and everything else would be AI agents. I'm not so sure it is possible," Abrahami said. "I think that we all give too much credit for AI and what it can do."
Even the man who coined the term vibe coding has been public about its many limitations for engineers.
In an April talk, former Tesla AI head and OpenAI founding member Andrej Karpathy said that code written by AI is still messy.
"Sometimes I get a little bit of a heart attack because it's not like super amazing code necessarily all the time," he said. "It's very bloaty, and there's a lot of copy-paste, and there's awkward abstractions that are brittle, and it works, but it's just really gross."

title: The 3 biggest takeaways from Mark Zuckerberg's media blitz
contentSnippet:
Mark Zuckerberg went on a media blitz with an open letter, an op-ed, and a NYT interview.
Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images

The Meta CEO went on a media blitz with an open letter, an op-ed, and a NYT interview.
Zuckerberg laid out a vision for AI to be open, widely distributed, and empowering.
Here are the biggest takeaways from Zuckerberg's public push to shape the AI conversation.

Mark Zuckerberg is making his biggest public push yet to shape the AI debate.
Within a week, the Meta CEO published an open letter, penned a Wall Street Journal op-ed, and sat down with The New York Times for a rare interview.
Across all three appearances, Zuckerberg laid out a consistent message: AI should be open, widely distributed, and built to empower individuals — not replace them.
Here are the three biggest takeaways from his media blitz.
AI shouldn't be centralized
Zuckerberg repeatedly said that concentrating advanced AI in the hands of a few companies would be both economically and politically dangerous.
In Zuckerberg's open letter, he said that America's "advantage is decentralized and open innovation," and that closing AI models to prevent China from gaining access to them will "only disadvantage the US and its allies."
Zuckerberg echoed that view in his New York Times interview.
"So much of the discourse from a lot of the other labs that are developing this is overwhelmingly filled with doom," Zuckerberg said. "There needs to be a voice or several voices that are bringing realism to this debate."
"I think it is literally impossible to have a single benevolent superintelligence that is simultaneously aligned with everyone at once," Zuckerberg added.
Zuckerberg doesn't think AI will kill jobs
Zuckerberg is not buying the AI job market pessimism
"I don't understand why anyone who believes that AI will eliminate most jobs and much of humanity's relevance would rush to build that future," said Zuckerberg in his essay in the Journal.
Instead, he said that broadly available AI will create "more jobs in the future, not fewer," making it easier to start businesses and fueling a more entrepreneurial economy.
Invention, not automation, is AI's biggest opportunity
Rather than framing AI primarily as a tool to automate work, Zuckerberg argued its greatest impact will come from helping people invent entirely new things.
"Invention, not automation, will be the greatest contribution of superintelligence," Zuckerberg wrote in the Journal, adding that AI could accelerate discoveries ranging from new medicines to breakthroughs that help people build businesses and solve problems.
"The history of democracy and economics has shown that there is no single objective answer to how people define the best life," Zuckerberg added, "And therefore the best approach is letting people decide what matters to them."

title: Zendaya says Tom Holland has a quality she wishes she had more of
contentSnippet:
Zendaya says Tom Holland is great at setting boundaries.
Christopher Polk/Deadline via Getty Images

Zendaya said there's one thing Tom Holland does better than she does.
Holland is "good at setting the boundaries really clearly, really strong," she said.
The pair recently shared the screen in "The Odyssey," and will reunite in the coming "Spider-Man" film.

Zendaya said Tom Holland is better than she is at setting boundaries.
Speaking alongside Holland in a joint interview with French YouTuber HugoDécrypte on Monday, Zendaya said she admired Holland's ability to draw clear lines and to stand up for himself and others.
"Something I am always impressed with Tom about, which I feel like I want to inherit more of," Zendaya said. "You're a big stickler for respect and kindness."
She said Holland makes his expectations around respect and kindness clear from the outset, then firmly enforces those boundaries if they're crossed.
On the other hand, she tends to be more conciliatory and more likely to smooth things over than draw a hard line, she said.
"You're good at setting the boundaries really clearly, really strong," Zendaya said.
"I like that you really know what you feel is right for yourself, and you do it, and for others. You're very protective in that way," Zendaya said.
True enough, when it was his turn to answer, Holland ended the exchange with a joke.
"Speaking of boundaries, I'm not going to share my most valuable piece of advice I got from Zendaya," he said.
The couple — and longtime costars — have previously spoken about the influence they've had on each other.
In a 2024 interview with Vanity Fair, Zendaya said it's "strangely comfortable" acting alongside Holland, with whom she's been in a public relationship since 2021.
"It's like second nature, if anything. You feel extra safe with the person you're acting beside. I love working with him. He's so talented, and so passionate about what he does. He always gives things one thousand percent, even if he's absolutely worn down," she said.
Earlier this month, Holland said he initially hesitated to accept a role in Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" because filming would overlap with "Spider-Man: Brand New Day." Zendaya, he said, jokingly told him she'd "leave" him if he turned it down.
The scheduling conflict was ultimately resolved after Sony delayed production, allowing the couple to appear in both films.
"The Odyssey" hit theaters on July 17, while "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" opens July 31.

title: Elon Musk's solar ambitions have shifted from powering homes to powering Tesla's AI era
contentSnippet:
Elon Musk has called for greater investment in solar energy to power AI infrastructure.
Marc Piasecki/Getty Images

Tesla inked deals to purchase electricity from two utility-scale solar power projects.
The projects have a combined solar capacity of roughly 600 megawatts.
Tesla's latest power purchases come as the company invests heavily in AI and robotics.

About a decade ago, Tesla entered its solar-for-homes era with its contentious acquisition of SolarCity.
Now, Tesla's solar dreams are taking a different shape as the company enters its AI era.
Tesla has inked two long-term agreements to purchase power from utility-scale solar projects totaling about 600 megawatts of planned capacity.
ContourGlobal, a global power producer, announced on Tuesday that Tesla signed a long-term agreement to purchase 1 terawatt-hour of electricity a year from Project Sterling, ContourGlobal's solar and battery storage project in Arizona. The deal covers about 90% of the project's expected output — roughly enough electricity to power about 100,000 US homes a year.
Renewable-energy developer Zelestra separately announced Tuesday that Tesla would purchase the entire output of its 140-megawatt Lumen Farm solar project in northeast Texas. Zelestra CEO Phil North said in a statement that the project will support Tesla's "growing energy needs in Texas."
The deals reflect Elon Musk's latest arc from leveraging solar power for consumer homes to solar use in industrial settings, which could include AI infrastructure.
Tesla's humble $2.6B solar beginnings
When the CEO proposed buying SolarCity, a rooftop solar installer and financier, in 2016, Musk framed the $2.6 billion deal as a way to create a seamless, end-to-end solution combining solar energy, battery storage, and EVs.
"Tesla customers can drive clean cars and they can use our battery packs to help consume energy more efficiently, but they still need access to the most sustainable energy source that's available: the sun," Tesla said at the time.
The rooftop solar business didn't disappear. Tesla said in its first-quarter shareholder update in April that it had begun "meaningful customer deployments" of residential solar panels produced at its New York Gigafactory. Tesla also continues to sell Powerwall batteries for homes.
Tesla produces solar panels at its Buffalo, New York, factory.
Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images

In recent years, however, Musk has increasingly focused his solar ambitions on the grid, as AI is expected to drive surging power demand and Tesla stakes more of its future on AI and robotics.
Tesla's AI bet relies on the sun
Tesla has warned investors that data centers supporting its AI services and products will have "substantial power requirements."
The company said in April that it expected 2026 capex to exceed $25 billion as it builds factories and infrastructure for projects including its Robotaxi business and the Optimus humanoid robot. Both ventures depend on large-scale AI training infrastructure. Tesla also plans to build a semiconductor research fab as part of its long shot chip manufacturing ambitions.
Musk has simultaneously been raising the stakes for industrial solar power amid the AI boom. In a January earnings call, the CEO said "the solar opportunity is underestimated," and that solar paired with batteries was the "best way" to add more power to the grid.
During Tesla's latest earnings call, on July 22, Musk said hyperscalers are struggling to secure enough electricity for AI compute, necessitating alternative energy sources.
"There's far more power available from the sun than anything else, by far," Musk said. "We think power constraints are going to be — they already are — a major issue for AI."
The two latest solar deals make Tesla a major buyer of utility-scale solar power. The EV maker has committed to purchasing nearly all of Project Sterling's annual electricity output and all of Zelestra's Lumen Farm output.
ContourGlobal said commercial operations are expected to start in 2028 and that Sterling will be the company's "largest renewable asset to date." Zelestra said it expects full operations to start by 2029.
Neither agreement identified which Tesla operations the power purchases will exactly support. Spokespeople for ContourGlobal, Zelestra, and Tesla did not respond to requests for comment.
As Musk's broader arc in solar energy has come into focus, solar is no longer powering only homes and cars but also the infrastructure of an AI-driven future.

title: ServiceNow cut hundreds of jobs to streamline operations. One staffer called it a 'very tough day.'
contentSnippet:
Bill McDermott, chief executive of ServiceNow
Bloomberg/Getty Images

ServiceNow cuts jobs, reflecting broader challenges in the software sector.
CEO Bill McDermott has urged staff to make workflows more efficient as a model for customers.
ServiceNow has made several large acquisitions this year.

ServiceNow has been cutting several hundred jobs as part of a global restructuring, the latest sign of pressure on the software industry.
A ServiceNow spokesperson said a "low single-digit" percentage of the company's total head count has been affected by the cuts, which have happened over several months this year.
ServiceNow ended 2025 with 29,187 employees, so the cuts likely total several hundred jobs.
CEO Bill McDermott said at the start of this year that ServiceNow would end 2026 with the same head count as it started the year with. He's also been pushing staff to reorganize their workflows to embrace new technology and be an example to ServiceNow customers on how to become more efficient.
ServiceNow has also made some big acquisitions in the past year, such as Armis and Veza, so the company is likely streamlining operations from integrating these new businesses.
One ServiceNow employee told Business Insider on Tuesday the cuts were described internally as a global restructuring and said it had been a "very tough day." This person asked not to be identified discussing sensitive matters.
Investors have hammered some software stocks in the past year on concerns that AI will disrupt the sector by reducing demand and making it easier for companies to develop their own software tools.
ServiceNow, like many enterprise software companies, is investing heavily in AI while reshaping parts of its business.
Last week, ServiceNow reported quarterly results that met or exceeded Wall Street expectations and raised its full-year subscription revenue guidance, even as investors continue to debate how AI will reshape the software industry.
